title: The Six Days of Creation
setting: Eden in the afternoon, where Raphael tells how the Son made the world out of Chaos
summary: Milton calls on Urania, the heavenly Muse, to guide the second half of his poem. Adam asks how the world began, and Raphael tells how God, answering the rebels’ fall, sent the Son to create a new world and a new race. The Son marks out the universe with golden compasses, and over six days light, sky, land and sea, plants, sun and stars, fish and birds, beasts and finally man and woman are made; on the seventh day Heaven celebrates the Sabbath.

sections.title: Invocation to Urania
sections.note: Milton asks his heavenly Muse to bring him safely back to earth after his flight through Heaven. He describes his own state, blind and endangered ‘on evil days’, and prays to find ‘fit audience, though few’.

sections.title: Adam asks how the world began
sections.note: Adam and Eve take in the story of the war with wonder. Still thirsty for knowledge, Adam asks how and why the visible world was made, and offers to keep the angel talking into the night.

sections.title: Knowledge within bounds
sections.note: Raphael agrees, but warns that some things God keeps secret. Knowledge is like food: taken without temperance it turns wisdom to folly.

sections.title: God resolves to create
sections.note: After the rebels fall, God declares that Satan has not emptied Heaven, and that he will repair the loss by making a new world and a race who may rise to Heaven by obedience. He sends his Word, the Son, to do it.

sections.title: The Son rides out
sections.note: The angels sing ‘Glory to the Most High’, and the Son rides forth with his chariots through Heaven’s gates, which swing open on golden hinges.

sections.title: The golden compasses
sections.note: At the edge of the raging abyss the Son commands ‘Silence, ye troubled Waves’. He takes golden compasses and draws the circumference of the world, and the Spirit broods over the waters, separating the life-giving from the dregs.

sections.title: First day: light
sections.note: Light springs from the deep and travels in a radiant cloud, since there is no sun yet. The angels sing the first evening and the first morning.

sections.title: Second day: the firmament
sections.note: God sets the firmament of air between the waters below and the waters above, keeping Chaos at a safe distance.

sections.title: Third day: land, seas, plants
sections.note: The waters rush away ‘as armies at the call of trumpet’ and the mountains heave up their bare backs. The earth then clothes itself with grass, flowers, vines and trees in a sudden burst of growth.

sections.title: Fourth day: sun, moon, stars
sections.note: God makes the sun and pours most of the light into it, a ‘great palace now of light’ from which the stars draw theirs. The sun rises with the dawn and the Pleiades dancing before him.

sections.title: Fifth day: fish and birds
sections.note: The seas swarm with fish, seals, dolphins and leviathan, ‘a moving land’. Birds hatch and fly: eagles, cranes in formation, the nightingale, the swan, the cock and the peacock.

sections.title: Sixth day: the beasts
sections.note: Animals climb out of the earth full-grown; the lion paws to free his hind parts from the soil. Ants, bees and the serpent follow, the serpent ‘not noxious, but obedient’ to Adam.

sections.title: The making of man
sections.note: One creature is still needed: one who stands upright, reasons and worships. God makes Adam from dust in his own image, blesses man and woman, and repeats the single command about the tree.

sections.title: Return to Heaven
sections.note: The Son rides back up to Heaven to the sound of harps, along the road that Adam sees at night as the Milky Way. On the seventh day God rests and Heaven fills with music.

sections.title: The Sabbath hymn
sections.note: The angels sing that to create is greater than to destroy, and that God turns even Satan’s evil to more good. They end by blessing mankind: ‘thrice happy, if they know their happiness’.

sections.title: Raphael invites more questions
sections.note: Raphael says Adam’s request is answered and invites any further question within human measure.

glosses.note: The classical Muse of astronomy, whose name means ‘heavenly’. Milton says he invokes the meaning, not the pagan goddess.
Pegasus, the winged horse of Greek myth, a traditional image of poetic inspiration.
From Proverbs 8, where Wisdom says she was with God before the creation, ‘rejoicing always before him’.
The hero who tried to ride Pegasus up to heaven, was thrown, and wandered alone on the Aleian plain (Iliad, Book 6). Milton fears a similar fall.
The visible universe, which seems to turn once a day; the rest of the poem stays within it rather than in Heaven.
Milton’s own situation after the monarchy was restored in 1660: blind, out of favour, and in real danger for having defended the king’s execution.
Orpheus, torn apart by the frenzied women followers of Bacchus on Mount Rhodope in Thrace. His mother, the Muse Calliope, could not save him.
Wonder, astonishment.
Completed (Latin absolvere, to finish).
‘Light-bearer’, the name of the morning star, given to Satan before his fall; Raphael compares his old brightness to that star.
Spread out and live more spaciously, now that the rebels have left room.
The name God gives himself to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14).
The angels sing the words later sung at Christ’s birth: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men’ (Luke 2:14).
Everlasting.
All-creating; Milton’s own coinage.
Drawn from Proverbs 8:27, ‘when he set a compass upon the face of the depth’. Blake later painted God with these compasses in ‘The Ancient of Days’.
Like tartar, the dregs that settle out of wine; with a hint of Tartarus, the classical pit of punishment.
The ‘fifth essence’: the pure heavenly element thought to lie beyond earth, water, air and fire.
Winding wandering (Latin errare, to wander), with no sense of mistake, though ‘serpent’ casts a shadow ahead.
Venus, which shows phases and ‘horns’ like a crescent moon, as Galileo’s telescope had shown.
The star cluster of the Seven Sisters. ‘Sweet influence’ recalls Job 38:31, ‘Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades?’
The great sea creature of Job 41, here a whale; in Book I Satan is compared to one.
Grew their full feathers, a falconer’s phrase.
The peacock’s tail, with its rainbow colours and ‘starry eyes’.
Dwells.
A lynx or snow leopard. The ‘libbard’ of the next line is a leopard, and ‘brinded’ means streaked.
The huge beast of Job 40, here taken to be the elephant.
The hippopotamus, which means ‘river horse’ in Greek.
Ant. Proverbs 6 holds up the ant as provident; Milton adds that its society may model a just commonwealth of equals.
Glassy; ‘the glassy sea’ before God’s throne in Revelation 4:6.

famous.why: Milton’s most personal lines: ‘fallen on evil days… In darkness, and with dangers compassed round’, ending with the wish for ‘fit audience, though few’.
‘Knowledge is as food’: Raphael’s compact image of why curiosity needs temperance.
The Son draws the world with golden compasses: ‘Thus far extend, thus far thy bounds’, an image Blake made famous.
The animals struggling out of the earth, the lion ‘pawing to get free his hinder parts’, is Milton at his most vivid and playful.
The ‘master-work’: man made upright, with reason, to look up and worship.

themes: Creation is joyful order out of chaos, measured, named and declared good.
God answers loss with making: ‘to create is greater than created to destroy’, and evil is turned to more good.
Curiosity is good but needs temperance; some things are not for humans to know.
The poet’s own darkness and danger sit beside the brightness of the first days.
art: The Son leaning from his chariot at the edge of dark, churning Chaos with golden compasses, one foot set at the center and the other sweeping the circle of the world.
